core: Crisis as a professional term: a time-limited state in which a person's usual coping is overwhelmed by an event or situation, not a diagnosis
Historical grounding: Lindemann's 1944 study of acute grief and Caplan's 1964 Principles of Preventive Psychiatry, including the critique that accompanied crisis theory from the start
Staged crisis models (Roberts and Ottens 2005) presented as teaching frameworks rather than validated procedures
Goals of crisis response: safety, stabilization, and connection to continuing support; why the work is explicitly time-limited and is not therapy
The current U.S. crisis system: the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, mobile crisis teams, stabilization services, and co-responder models, organized by SAMHSA's three foundational elements
De-escalation as professional posture and communication, and the limits of its randomized evidence base
Least-restrictive response, and why involuntary intervention is a last resort governed by state law and institutional policy that vary
What happens after a crisis contact: handoff to continuing services, documentation under agency policy, and the workforce conditions that bear on staff well-being
supporting: 988 operational facts: launch timeline, contact modalities, network of local crisis centers, language access
Evidence status of mobile crisis units in the United States
Evidence on co-responder programs and involuntary detention
Inconsistent definitions of 'voluntary' and 'involuntary' in U.S. behavioral health services
outOfScope: Any risk-assessment, screening, or safety-planning protocol
Individualized clinical, diagnostic, legal, or safety advice
Any description of methods of self-harm or vivid depiction of a crisis
The SAMHSA trauma-informed framework and re-traumatization (owned by trauma-informed-care)
The physiological stress response, PTSD diagnosis and treatment, and resilience (owned by stress-trauma-and-resilience)
Grief theory and bereavement counseling beyond Lindemann's historical role

claims.claim: In the crisis literature, a crisis is described as an ordinary human reaction to severe psychosocial stress or to a situation in which a person is overwhelmed and their usual coping breaks down, and crises are treated as temporary, episodic phenomena rather than as chronic illness.

Crisis theory traces to Eric Lindemann's 1944 paper on the symptomatology and management of acute grief in the American Journal of Psychiatry, and to Gerald Caplan's Principles of Preventive Psychiatry (Tavistock, 1964), which drew on Lindemann's crisis theory and argued that help concentrated on people facing a developmental or accidental hazard involving loss, threat, or challenge has maximum impact because short-term intervention arrives at a point where growth or breakdown may follow.

Criticism of crisis theory is as old as the theory: a 1965 review of Caplan's book warned that the framework was convenient enough for community planning that it might be accepted too uncritically, and questioned whether the effects of crisis intervention would outlast the crisis itself.

Roberts and Ottens published a seven-stage crisis intervention model in Brief Treatment and Crisis Intervention in 2005, framed in its own title as a road map to goal attainment, problem solving, and crisis resolution.

SAMHSA's National Behavioral Health Crisis Care Guidance is built on three foundational elements: Someone to Contact (services such as the 988 Lifeline and other behavioral health hotlines), Someone to Respond (mobile crisis teams delivering rapid on-site intervention and connection to care, plus crisis outreach teams for prevention and postvention), and A Safe Place for Help (an array of stabilization services). The guidance comprises two finalized 2025 documents, the National Guidelines for a Behavioral Health Coordinated System of Crisis Care and Model Definitions for Behavioral Health Emergency, Crisis, and Crisis-Related Services.

The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is a free, confidential, 24/7 phone, chat, and text service reached anywhere in the United States, operated through a national network of more than 200 local, independent crisis centers staffed by trained crisis counselors, with Spanish-language and Deaf/Hard-of-Hearing services and interpretation in more than 240 additional languages, and with a subnetwork connecting veterans and service members to the Veterans Crisis Line.

988 is intended for thoughts of suicide, mental health or substance use crises, and emotional distress generally, and people can contact it about themselves or because they are worried about someone else; it is not restricted to imminent suicidal crisis.

The FCC issued its final order designating 988 on July 16, 2020, requiring U.S. telecommunications providers to activate 988 by July 16, 2022, and the country transitioned to the three-digit code in July 2022; the predecessor National Suicide Prevention Lifeline launched in 2005, and Spanish-language text and chat and Deaf/Hard-of-Hearing videophone service were added in 2023.

SAMHSA describes the longer-term aim of 988 as linking people who call, text, or chat to community-based providers who can deliver a fuller range of crisis services, such as mobile crisis teams or stabilization centers, in addition to prevention resources — that is, the contact is an entry point, not the whole intervention.

A Cochrane review of single-session psychological debriefing found no evidence that it prevents PTSD: pooled short-term results showed no significant reduction in PTSD risk, one trial reported a significantly increased risk of PTSD at one year among those who received debriefing (odds ratio 2.88, 95% CI 1.11 to 7.53), and the reviewers concluded that compulsory debriefing of trauma victims should stop.

The 2023 VA/DoD clinical practice guideline for PTSD and acute stress disorder states that for the prevention of PTSD among trauma-exposed individuals there is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against psychotherapy or pharmacotherapy in the immediate post-trauma period, and its evidence review notes that Critical Incident Stress Debriefing delivered immediately after trauma exposure did not reduce PTSD incidence at six-month follow-up.

De-escalation is described as a psychosocial intervention for managing disturbed or aggressive behavior, with secondary strategies such as rapid tranquillisation, physical intervention, and seclusion considered only after de-escalation and other strategies have failed; a Cochrane review searching to April 2016 found no randomized trials meeting inclusion criteria, so the practice is standard without randomized support.

A 2025 systematic review of U.S. mobile crisis units found that despite nearly two thousand active services, only nine studies since 2000 met inclusion criteria; results were mixed, the review concluded that the evidence offers tentative support but is too sparse for firm or generalized conclusions, and it noted that the previous review, in 1995, found no evidence of effectiveness. The review identified hospital diversion, justice-system diversion, and accessible community-based patient-centered care as the primary functions of mobile crisis units.

A quasi-experimental study of a U.S. co-responder program, which pairs mental health professionals with police officers on qualified emergency calls, found a 16.5% reduction in involuntary psychiatric detentions (370 fewer over two years) with no detectable effect on program-related calls for service, criminal offences, or arrests.

Decisions about involuntary treatment in the United States are guided by state laws and institutional policies, and a 2026 scoping review found that U.S. health professionals do not define 'voluntary' and 'involuntary' consistently, so no single national rule can be stated in a lesson.

Staffing conditions in the 988 network are strained: in a 2025 survey of all 206 network centers with a 77% response rate (159 of 206), 71% of leaders answering that item (102 of 144) reported their center was understaffed and 89% (141 of 159) reported difficulty acquiring resources to hire, and the authors concluded that persistent staffing challenges could put staff well-being and service quality at risk.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Dating of the Lindemann and Caplan contributions
positions: A 2025 BMC Psychiatry article states that 'early work by Gerard Caplan in the 1940s and Eric Lindeman in the 1960s' shaped crisis intervention theory.

The bibliographic record for Lindemann's acute-grief paper places it in the American Journal of Psychiatry in 1944, and a contemporaneous 1965 review places Caplan's Principles of Preventive Psychiatry at Tavistock in 1964, drawing on Lindemann's crisis theory.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the primary bibliographic records: Lindemann 1944, Caplan 1964, with Caplan building on Lindemann. The secondary article's ordering and dates appear to be transposed and were not used.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether crisis models such as staged frameworks are validated procedures
positions: Staged models are widely taught and cited in crisis practice literature.

Targeted searching of the peer-reviewed literature surfaced no systematic review establishing the effectiveness of any specific staged crisis intervention sequence; the most-cited model is presented by its own authors as a road map.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson labels staged models as teaching frameworks, states plainly that their staged sequences are not backed by review-level evidence, and does not enumerate stages as if they were a procedure.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Strength of evidence for mobile crisis units
positions: Mobile crisis units are funded and deployed at scale in the U.S. as a core part of the crisis continuum.
The 2025 systematic review found nine qualifying studies with mixed results and concluded the literature is too sparse for firm conclusions.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports both the scale of deployment and the thinness of the evidence, and does not describe mobile crisis units as an evidence-based practice.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive content about crisis intervention: its In 30 Seconds, College Version, vocabulary, worked example, and mistakes were topic-neutral boilerplate ('a foundational concept in Social Work & Human Services', 'a label on a toolbox drawer') and supported nothing.
The draft's vocabulary entry defining the topic in terms of itself was circular and was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with researched content.

Used SAMHSA's current (2025) wording for the three foundational elements — Someone to Contact, Someone to Respond, A Safe Place for Help — rather than the older 'someone to talk to / someone to respond / a safe place to go' phrasing that circulates in secondary sources.
Omitted the ABC model of crisis intervention: no authoritative or peer-reviewed source for it could be verified within this session's research constraints, so it was cut rather than asserted.

Did not enumerate the stages of Roberts and Ottens' model, both because the full text was not accessible and because a stage list would read as an intervention protocol, which this lesson deliberately avoids.
Stated the debriefing evidence as a correction to a widely held belief, including the one-year increased-risk finding, rather than the softer 'debriefing is no longer recommended'.
Avoided any claim that de-escalation is evidence-based; the Cochrane review found no qualifying randomized trials.
rightsIssues: SAMHSA's 2025 National Guidelines PDF and Model Definitions PDF are behind a bot-protection layer on library.samhsa.gov and could not be retrieved; only the SAMHSA webpage summarizing them was read, and the lesson claims nothing beyond what that page states.
988lifeline.org is operated by Vibrant Emotional Health and its content is copyrighted; recorded REFERENCE_ONLY and no wording reproduced.
Cochrane reviews are subscription content; only the structured abstracts available through Europe PMC were read, and both are recorded REFERENCE_ONLY.
Two peer-reviewed sources carry CC BY-NC-ND licenses, which permit no derivatives; both are recorded REFERENCE_ONLY and only facts, not wording, were used.
All prose in the lesson is original EliExplains writing; no source sentence was paraphrase-followed.

sourceRecords.title: Psychological debriefing for preventing post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2002, Issue 2, CD000560)
sourceRecords.provider: Rose S, Bisson J, Churchill R, Wessely S; record and structured abstract via PubMed (PMID 12076399)
sourceRecords.notes: Eleven randomized trials of single-session debriefing met inclusion criteria; trial quality was generally poor. No significant short-term (3-5 month) reduction in PTSD risk (OR 1.22, 95% CI 0.60-2.46); one trial reported significantly increased PTSD risk at one year (OR 2.88, 95% CI 1.11-7.53); no evidence of reduced general psychological morbidity, depression, or anxiety. Reviewers concluded there is no evidence debriefing prevents PTSD and that compulsory debriefing of trauma victims should cease. This is the anchor for the lesson's Common Mistakes correction. Only the structured abstract was read; the full review is subscription content.

sourceRecords.title: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Acute Stress Disorder (June 2023)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and U.S. Department of Defense, Evidence-Based Practice Work Group
sourceRecords.notes: Full 167-page PDF retrieved and text-extracted. Used for the guideline's stated position that, for prevention of PTSD among trauma-exposed individuals, there is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against psychotherapy or pharmacotherapy in the immediate post-trauma period, and for its evidence discussion noting that Critical Incident Stress Debriefing administered immediately after trauma exposure did not reduce PTSD incidence at six-month follow-up in blinded randomized trials in civilian samples. Corroborates, from current federal guidance, the Cochrane finding used in Common Mistakes.

sourceRecords.title: De-escalation techniques for psychosis-induced aggression or agitation (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2017, CD009922)
sourceRecords.provider: Du M, Wang X, Yin S, Shu W, Hao R, Zhao S, Rao H, Yeung WL, Jayaram MB, Xia J; record and structured abstract via PubMed (PMID 28368091)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the review's framing of de-escalation as a psychosocial intervention used before secondary strategies such as rapid tranquillisation, physical intervention, and seclusion, and its central finding: of 345 citations identified in searches to April 2016, none was an includable randomized trial, so no data could be extracted. Used in the lesson to state that de-escalation is standard recommended practice without randomized support, and to teach the distinction between absent evidence and evidence of absence.

sourceRecords.title: Mobile crisis effectiveness: a systematic review and associated functions and forms framework (BMC Health Services Research, 2025)
sourceRecords.provider: Peters RL, Fine J, Newton H, Dalack GW, Watson A, Lich KH; PubMed Central (PMC12801951)
sourceRecords.license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 as recorded in Europe PMC
sourceRecords.notes: DOI 10.1186/s12913-025-13806-2. Source for the scale-versus-evidence gap: nearly two thousand mobile crisis units active in the U.S.; the previous review (1995) found no evidence of effectiveness; nine of 134 screened studies met inclusion criteria for this review, with mixed findings; the authors conclude the evidence offers tentative support but is too sparse for firm or generalized conclusions. Also the source for the primary functions of mobile crisis units: hospital diversion, justice-system diversion, and accessible patient-centered care in the community. No-derivatives license, so facts only were used.

sourceRecords.title: Emergency mental health co-responders reduce involuntary psychiatric detentions in the USA (Nature Human Behaviour, 2026)
sourceRecords.provider: Dee TS, Pyne J; PubMed Central (PMC12846909)
sourceRecords.license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 as recorded in Europe PMC
sourceRecords.notes: DOI 10.1038/s41562-025-02339-7. Two quasi-experimental designs of a co-responder program pairing mental health professionals with police on qualified emergency calls: 16.5% reduction in involuntary psychiatric detentions (370 fewer over two years; b = -0.180, 95% CI -0.325 to -0.034), with no detectable effect on program-related calls for service, criminal offences, or arrests. Also the source for the historical framing that deinstitutionalization left police as typical first responders to mental health emergency calls.

sourceRecords.title: The Seven-Stage Crisis Intervention Model: A Road Map to Goal Attainment, Problem Solving, and Crisis Resolution (Brief Treatment and Crisis Intervention, 5(4), 329-339)
sourceRecords.provider: Roberts AR, Ottens AJ; bibliographic record verified via Crossref (DOI 10.1093/brief-treatment/mhi030)
sourceRecords.notes: Bibliographic record only: title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages, and year confirmed through the Crossref API. Used to attribute the best-known staged crisis model accurately and to note that its own title presents it as a road map. Full text was not accessible, so the lesson does not enumerate or describe the individual stages, and makes no claim about the model's effectiveness.

sourceRecords.title: Book review: Principles of Preventive Psychiatry by Gerald Caplan (Mental Health (London), 24(4), 1965, p. 174)
sourceRecords.provider: Guise-Moores S, National Association for Mental Health; PubMed Central (PMC5085475)
sourceRecords.notes: Contemporaneous review confirming that Caplan's Principles of Preventive Psychiatry was published by Tavistock in 1964, that its approach drew on Lindemann's crisis theory, that it located helping leverage in people facing a developmental or accidental hazard involving loss, threat, or challenge where short-term intervention has maximum impact, and that a reader in 1965 already warned the framework might be accepted too uncritically and doubted whether crisis intervention's effects would outlast the crisis. Used for historical grounding and for the lesson's point that the critique is as old as the theory. Paraphrased; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Symptomatology and management of acute grief (American Journal of Psychiatry, 1944; reprinted 151(6 Suppl), 1994, 155-160)
sourceRecords.notes: Bibliographic record confirming author, title, journal, original 1944 date, and the 1994 sesquicentennial reprint (DOI 10.1176/ajp.151.6.155). Used only to date and attribute the origin of the acute-grief work that crisis theory was built on; no content claims are drawn from the paper itself, which was not accessible.

sourceRecords.title: Using Crisis Theory in Dealing With Severe Mental Illness - A Step Toward Normalization? (Frontiers in Sociology, 7, 805604, 2022)
sourceRecords.provider: Baumgardt J, Weinmann S; PubMed Central (PMC9218753)
sourceRecords.notes: DOI 10.3389/fsoc.2022.805604. Full text read. Supports the lesson's account of crisis as a temporal and episodic phenomenon rather than a chronic, biologically driven condition; the framing of a crisis as a possible turning point; the observation that a crisis framing is less prone to medicalization than a diagnostic framing; and the caution that crisis theory was developed with people without severe mental illness in mind and needs modification before it is applied to that population.

sourceRecords.title: Effect of crisis resolution team treatment on crisis experience and crisis coping: a multicenter pre-post study in Norway (BMC Psychiatry, 25(1), 1067, 2025)
sourceRecords.provider: Holgersen KH, Hasselberg N, Siqveland J, Ruud T; PubMed Central (PMC12593888)
sourceRecords.notes: DOI 10.1186/s12888-025-07491-y. Full text read. Supports the working definition used in the lesson - crises described in both the disaster literature and the crisis-team literature as ordinary human reactions to severe psychosocial stressors, or situations where a person is overwhelmed and usual coping breaks down - and the statement that general crisis theory underpins the development of crisis resolution teams while little research has examined what actually happens in these contacts. The article's dating of Lindemann and Caplan is transposed and was not relied on.

sourceRecords.title: "Involuntary" and "Voluntary" in Psychiatric, Behavioral, and Mental Health Services: A Scoping Review of Definitions (Journal of Behavioral Health Services & Research, 53(1), 142-164, 2026)
sourceRecords.provider: Smart BD, Kalathil K, McCall WV, Munjal S, Kirkendall H, Patel M, Taliaferro A, Yaeger LH, Iltis AS; PubMed Central (PMC12876088)
sourceRecords.notes: DOI 10.1007/s11414-025-09940-8. Full text read. Supports two claims: that clinical decisions about involuntary treatment in the U.S. are usually guided by state laws and institutional policies, and that the meaning of voluntary and involuntary lacks shared definition across U.S. behavioral health practice - the basis for the lesson's refusal to state a national rule and its instruction that students learn their own jurisdiction's law under supervision.

sourceRecords.title: Workforce and Staffing at 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline Centers (JAMA Network Open, 2026)
sourceRecords.provider: Matthews S, Holliday SB, Slover R, Liu J, Breslau J, Purtle J, Kilambi V, Schuler MS, Ramchand R, Cantor J, McBain RK; PubMed Central (PMC13147195)
sourceRecords.notes: DOI 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.10789. Cross-sectional survey fielded May 6 to July 25, 2025 to all 206 centers in the 988 network, 77% response rate: 71% of responding leaders reported the center was understaffed and 89% reported difficulty acquiring resources to hire, with the authors concluding that persistent staffing challenges could threaten staff well-being and service quality. Used for the lesson's closing point that the conditions crisis workers work under are a system-design question, not only a personal-resilience question.
